newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Mobutu departure opens way for peace.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Mobutu departure opens way for peace.

text.p: The United States said on Friday the departure of President Mobutu Sese Seko from Kinshasa made possible a peaceful end to the Zaire conflict.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told reporters: "We believe that his departure now opens the way for a peaceful resolution of the military conflict."
She and President Bill Clinton said the United States priority was to see a peaceful transition to a democratic government in the huge, chaotic central African state.
Clinton pledged to "do what we can to support Africa in taking one of the the largest and most important nations in Africa and promoting a democratic transition. That is what I think is important."

As rebel forces advanced towards Kinshasa, Mobutu left the capital on Friday for his native village in northern Zaire and an official statement said he would no longer take any part in the government of the country.
The Clinton administration has been saying for weeks that the era of Mobutu is over, making clear it has withdrawn support for the autocratic leader.

Washington and other western states backed Mobutu for decades as he upheld their interests in African struggles that were often proxy battles between the major western and communist powers in the Cold War.

"We are at this stage working with all the parties so that we can avoid bloodshed and also to do what can be done in terms of contributing to a process that would be peaceful and have an inclusive transition that would result in free and fair elections," Albright said.
"I think the most important point here is that Zaire now needs to move forward away from war towards peace, stability and elections," she added.
Clinton urged worldwide support for the efforts of South African leader Nelson Mandela to end the violence.
He told reporters at the White House that Mandela had done "a superb job" in trying to end the fighting. "I want the whole world to get behind him," he said.
"The United States' position is clear," Clinton said. "We want to see a transition to a genuine democracy."
He pledged to "do what we can to support Africa in taking one of the the largest and most important nations in Africa and promoting a democratic transition. That is what I think is important."

Mandela has consulted regularly with African leaders and the British, U.S. and French governments in his efforts to avert a military showdown in Kinshasa between Mobutu's government forces and Laurent Kabila's rebel army.
But neither he nor Clinton's special envoy, U.N. Ambassador Bill Richardson, have succeeded in persuading Mobuto and Kabila to accept a negotiated settlement and stop the fighting.
